readerTitle: Why the big rival won't copy you, even when it easily could
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가전 체인 vs 신생 창고형 판매점, 사내 교육팀) + 실제 기업 (Vanguard 인덱스 펀드)
insight: 가장 강한 방어벽은 내가 가진 것이 아니라, 경쟁자가 나를 따라 하면 자기 사업을 해치게 되는 구조일 수 있다.
misconception: 대기업이 신생 기업을 따라 하지 않는 것은 위협을 못 보거나 게을러서다. 돈과 규모가 더 많은 쪽이 결국 이긴다.

sources.text: Helmer, H. (2016). 7 Powers: The Foundations of Business Strategy. (Counter-positioning 개념과 Vanguard 사례)
Vanguard, company history (1975 founding, first index mutual fund offered to individual investors, fund-owned structure)
가전 체인, 사내 교육팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Vanguard 설립(1975년, John Bogle)과 개인 투자자용 첫 인덱스 뮤추얼 펀드 출시(1976년) 연도를 Vanguard 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "in the 1970s"로만 적었습니다.
Vanguard가 펀드(즉 펀드 투자자)가 소유하는 구조라는 점을 공식 자료로 확인하세요.
기존 운용사들이 인덱스 펀드에 오래 소극적이었다는 서술은 Helmer(2016)의 설명에 근거합니다. 특정 회사 이름이나 연도, 시장 점유율 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 일부 운용사는 결국 인덱스 펀드를 출시했으므로 "slow to push them hard"로 표현했습니다.
가전 체인의 매장 수(40개)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The big chain could copy the newcomer tomorrow. It won't.
body: Picture two appliance sellers in one city. One is a chain with 40 showrooms and salespeople paid on commission. The other is a newcomer: one warehouse, a website, fixed low prices, no haggling.
The chain has more money, more stores and a better-known name. It can see exactly what the newcomer does. And it still doesn't copy it.

image.label: A large showroom facing a small warehouse across a street
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 크고 화려한 가전 쇼룸(정장 차림 판매원들), 오른쪽에 작고 단순한 창고("Fixed low prices" 간판, 박스 더미). 쇼룸 창문 안에서 누군가 창고를 쳐다보고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: You run the chain.
body: The newcomer is winning younger customers. Your profits depend on showroom sales at full prices. Your best salespeople earn most of their pay from commission.

options.text: Copy the model: fixed low prices, smaller commissions
options.feedback: You meet the threat head-on. But you cut the margin on every sale you already make, and your top sellers may leave.

options.text: Launch a separate low-price brand online
options.feedback: It shields the core business. But your stores may see it as a rival, because each sale it wins may be one a showroom loses.

options.text: Hold steady and promote expert advice in store
options.feedback: You keep today's profits. If customers keep moving, though, you're defending a business that shrinks each year.

choice.afterReveal: Every option costs the chain something it already has. That cost is what protects the newcomer.

cards.title: Same idea, very different price to pay.
body: For the newcomer, low fixed prices are the whole plan. For the chain, the same move means **less money from every customer it already has**.

breakdown.label: Showroom costs
breakdown.detail: Rent and staff paid for by higher prices

breakdown.label: Existing customers
breakdown.detail: Would pay less for the same fridge

breakdown.label: What the newcomer loses
breakdown.detail: It has no old model to protect

cards.title: Counter-positioning
body: **Counter-positioning** is when a newcomer picks a business model that the leader could copy, but copying would damage the leader's existing business.

Strategist Hamilton Helmer named it in his 2016 book *7 Powers*. The odd part: the moat isn't something the newcomer owns. It's the leader's own reluctance, and that reluctance is a rational choice, not laziness.

image.label: A rival holding a key, standing in front of its own house
image.brief: 개념 일러스트. 큰 회사 캐릭터가 신생 회사의 문을 열 열쇠를 들고 있지만, 그 열쇠를 쓰면 자기 집 기둥이 무너지는 그림. 기둥에 "Today's profits" 라벨.

cards.title: Vanguard and the fund industry
body: Helmer's main example is Vanguard. In the 1970s it began offering index funds to ordinary investors: funds that simply track the market, with very low fees. Vanguard is owned by its funds, so it had no outside owners demanding high fees.

Big fund companies could have done the same. Many were slow to push index funds hard, because every dollar moving into a cheap index fund was a dollar leaving a pricier fund they already ran. That hesitation gave Vanguard years to grow.

cards.title: Not every cheaper rival has it.
body: Being cheaper or better is not enough. If the leader can match you without hurting itself, it will, and your edge disappears.
The test is one question: **would copying you hurt their current business?** If yes, you may have counter-positioning. If no, you just have a head start.
cards.softwareNote: Software companies that sold one-time licences often hesitated to switch to subscriptions, because the move cut revenue in the short term. Newcomers that started with subscriptions had no such pain.

cards.title: This protection has an expiry date.
body: Counter-positioning lasts only while the old model stays worth protecting. Once it shrinks enough, or new leaders decide to take the pain, the incumbent copies you.
And the new model must really serve customers better. A model that rivals avoid only because it loses money is not a moat. It's a trap.
Finally, success turns you into an incumbent with your own model to protect.

cards.title: Now you're the one being counter-positioned.
body: You lead the training team inside a large company. Your budget comes from charging other departments per classroom day. An outside app offers short self-paced lessons per employee, and department heads are starting to use it.

options.text: Argue that classroom training is higher quality and keep your model
options.feedback: It protects this year's budget. But you're choosing your funding model over what departments now want.

options.text: Build a self-paced option and change how your team is funded
options.feedback: It costs you classroom days, but it removes the reason you'd resist the better option. That's the only real way out of counter-positioning.

options.text: Add videos, but keep charging per classroom day
options.feedback: You offer something similar. But your team still earns more when people choose classrooms, so the videos will get less effort.

cards.title: Your best edge can be a rival's own business model.
body: Look for what the leader can't copy without hurting itself. And if you are the leader, notice which good ideas you avoid only to protect today's revenue.
**Try it today:** write down where your biggest rival makes most of its money. What could you offer that would cost them that money to copy?
